beats.intro: Chapter three, lesson two. Primary and secondary structure. [[cord]]Think of a telephone cord, coiled up neatly. [[fan]]And a paper fan, pleated back and forth. Both are just a long strip, folded in a regular way. [[strip]]A protein chain does the same. Here is our strip of the four levels of protein structure. Today we light the first two: the plain chain, and the first folding, held by hydrogen bonds.
beats.primary: [[chain]]Primary structure is the number, type and sequence of the amino acids in the polypeptide chain. Like beads on a string, where the order of the colors matters. [[bond]]The main bond is the peptide bond, carbonyl then N H, that links each bead to the next. [[nend]]One end of the chain carries the free amino group of the first amino acid. That is the N-terminal end. [[cend]]The other end carries the free carboxyl group of the last amino acid. That is the C-terminal end. [[count]]And we always count the amino acids from the N-terminal end. This one is number one, and this one is number twenty.
beats.change: [[eight]]Why does the sequence matter? Because it is the whole recipe. Here are the first eight amino acids of one chain of hemoglobin, counted from the N-terminal end. [[swap]]In sickle-cell disease, the sixth amino acid is changed. Glutamic acid is replaced by valine. Just one bead out of hundreds. [[defect]]That one change makes the hemoglobin clump, and red blood cells bend into a sickle. So a change in one amino acid can cause a physiological defect. Not every change does, but this one does.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which end of the chain is amino acid number one?
beats.secondary: [[back]]Now secondary structure. The primary chain does not stay stretched out. Look at the backbone. Every peptide bond has an oxygen on its carbonyl carbon, and a hydrogen on its nitrogen. [[fold]]The chain folds, held by hydrogen bonds between these specific atoms of the backbone. Not the side chains. Just the backbone. Depending on where the bonds form, the chain takes one of two shapes: the alpha helix, or the beta sheet.
beats.helix: [[coil]]First, the alpha helix. The chain coils like the telephone cord, and it is a right-handed helix. [[turn]]Each turn contains three point six amino acids. One full turn is about point five four nanometers long. [[hb]]The hydrogen bond runs inside the same chain. It joins the carbonyl oxygen of one peptide bond to the hydrogen on the nitrogen four places further along. So amino acid one bonds with amino acid five, two with six, three with seven. [[stack]]Because of that, the bonds line up along the helix like rungs, and hold the coil firm. This is an intrachain hydrogen bond.
beats.q2: Quick check. In an alpha helix, the carbonyl oxygen of amino acid one bonds with the N H of which amino acid?
beats.sheet: [[pleat]]Second, the beta sheet. Here the chain is pleated, zigzag, like the paper fan, and the strands lie side by side. [[strands]]Hydrogen bonds link neighbouring strands, again from the carbonyl oxygen of one to the N H of the next. [[intra]]If both strands belong to one chain, folded back on itself, we call it an intrachain bond, between different segments of the same chain. [[inter]]If the strands belong to two adjacent chains, it is an interchain bond. Same bond, two cases. [[par]]The strands can run in the same direction, N to C, N to C. That is a parallel sheet. [[anti]]Or they can alternate, one up, one down. That is an antiparallel sheet.
beats.compare: [[table]]Let's compare. In both, the hydrogen bonds join backbone atoms, never the side chains. [[h]]The helix is a coil, with three point six amino acids per turn, and bonds inside the same chain, four places along. [[b]]The sheet is a pleat, with strands side by side, and bonds between the strands. [[levels]]And both sit above the primary level, which they leave untouched: the peptide bonds, and the sequence, are the same.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids, joined by peptide bonds, counted from the N-terminal end to the C-terminal end. One changed amino acid can cause disease. [[s2]]Secondary structure is the chain folded by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms. [[s3]]The alpha helix is a right-handed coil, three point six amino acids per turn, bonded within the chain. [[s4]]The beta sheet is pleated strands side by side, bonded between strands, parallel or antiparallel. [[end]]Now try the practice.
